extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners designing/evaluating conference peer-review assignment algorithms (e.g., ML conference program chairs, algorithm designers, peer-review systems researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating algorithms that assign reviewers to conference papers to (approximately) recover the top-k papers under various statistical models and similarity structures. Includes theoretical minimax guarantees and empirical metrics for assignment quality and downstream acceptance accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: k-separation threshold ∆k
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: if the difference between kth and (k+1)th papers is large enough, it should be easy to recover top k papers. Used as the central quantity controlling exact top-k recoverability; appears in sufficient and necessary (converse) conditions for recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family F_k(δ) of papers' scores
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to state uniform (worst-case) recovery guarantees: theorems consider sup over θ* in Fk(δ). Sets the hypothesis class under which probability bounds are derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundedness and monotonicity of h (reviewer noise function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume function h is bounded, h : [0,1] → [0,1], and monotonically decreasing. (Assumption before Theorem 3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption implies every reviewer can provide a minimum level of expertise even if similarity sij = 0. The paper also treats unbounded h later (h : [0,1] → [0,∞)) and extends results to sub-Gaussian noise; monotonic decrease captures 'higher similarity → lower noise'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity-family S(q) defined by fairness threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: S(q) := { S ∈ [0,1]^{n×m} : Γ_S^{1−h} ≥ q }. (Equation 16 and explanation)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: if similarity matrix S belongs to S(q), then the fairness of the optimally fair assignment (with respect to f = 1−h) is at least q. The tractability of top-k recovery depends on q; q must lie in [λ (1−h(0)), λ] for non-vacuous results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation factor τ_q
rubrics_metrics.description: τ_q := inf_{S∈S(q)} ( Γ_S^{1−h}(APR4A) / Γ_S^{1−h}(AHARD) ). (Equation 17)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures quality of approximation provided by PeerReview4All relative to optimal (AHARD). Theorem 1 gives lower bounds on τ_q. Worst-case τ_q ≥ 1/λ, but in many practical similarity matrices τ_q can be much better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient condition (Theorem 3) for exact top-k recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: For monotonically decreasing h : [0,1]→[0,1], q ∈ [λ(1−h(0)), λ], and α ∈ (0,1/4), if δ exceeds a function of (λ − q τ_q), ln m, λ and α then for APR4A with θ_MEAN and θ_MLE (constructed appropriately) we have P(estimated top-k = true top-k) ≥ 1−α. (Theorem 3(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem gives explicit δ thresholds (dependent on τ_q, q, λ, ln m) that guarantee exact recovery with high probability. A converse (Theorem 3(b)) provides matching lower bounds (up to constants and τ_q factor), establishing near-minimax optimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimator selection: θ_MLE versus θ_MEAN
rubrics_metrics.description: θ_MLE is preferred when the (Gaussian) model (11) is correct; θ_MEAN is more robust to model mismatches, especially when h(s) ∈ [0,1]. (Remarks after Theorem 3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: use θ_MLE when confident in the generative noise model; otherwise θ_MEAN may be safer. In the subjective-score model, θ_MEAN is the natural estimator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to sub-Gaussian noise
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper bound of Theorem 3 holds for a more general reviewer noise model y_{ij} = θ*_{j} + s_G(h(s_{ij})) where s_G is mean-zero sub-Gaussian with scale parameter σ^2. (Remark 5)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theoretical guarantees are not limited to Gaussian noise; they extend to sub-Gaussian noise, increasing practical applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family S_κ(v) parameterizing 'strong reviewer' structure
rubrics_metrics.description: S_κ(v) := { S ∈ [0,1]^{n×m} : s*_κ ≥ v }, where s*_κ defined earlier (Equation 20 and following text)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here v defines the threshold for 'strong' reviewer similarity and κ denotes the maximum number of strong reviewers that can be assigned to each paper (κ ∈ [λ]). This family models structures from worst-case (few strong reviewers) to ideal (λ strong reviewers per paper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive minimax optimality for S_κ(v) (Corollary 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any v∈[0,1], κ∈[λ] and monotonically decreasing h : [0,1]→[0,∞), if δ > function involving h(v), h(0), κ, (λ−κ), ln m then APR4A with θ_MLE achieves exact top-k recovery (probability ≥ 1−α) without an approximation factor. (Corollary 4(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: PeerReview4All with θ_MLE is simultaneously minimax (near-)optimal across a broad family of similarity-structure classes S_κ(v). This shows adaptivity to the underlying S structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized separation threshold ∆_{k,t} for Hamming-error recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: ∆_{k,t} := θ*_{(k−t)} − θ*_{(k+t+1)}; used when allowing Hamming error tolerance t. (Section 6.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When boundary scores are close, exact recovery may be impossible; ∆_{k,t} is the key quantity controlling approximate recovery guarantees under Hamming distance tolerance t.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamming distance DH as approximate recovery metric
rubrics_metrics.description: DH(T_k(A,θ), T*_k) measures closeness between accepted set and true top-k using Hamming distance; interest is in bounding P(DH > 2t) for user-defined t ∈ [k−1]. (Section 6.3.2 and Theorem 5)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorems provide sufficient and necessary δ thresholds (involving τ_q, q, λ, ln m, and t) that control the probability the Hamming error exceeds 2t.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimax characterization / approximation gap dependence on τ_q
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper and lower bounds for both exact and approximate recovery differ by the approximation factor τ_q (and constant pre-factors). (Remarks after Theorem 3 and Theorem 5)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: PeerReview4All's performance is near-minimax up to τ_q; improving τ_q (i.e., producing assignments closer to AHARD) tightens guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective-score model (full-competence reviewer scores Θ_{ij})
rubrics_metrics.description: Model: imagine fully-competent reviewer i would give score θ_{ij}; real-world observed y_{ij} ∼ N(θ_{ij}, h(s_{ij})). The goal is to recover top-k in terms of mean full-competence subjective scores θ̄_j = (1/λ) ∑_{i∈RA(j)} θ_{ij}. (Section 7.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separates subjective reviewer-specific opinions (Θ) from noise; assignment aims to ensure reviewers can convey their subjective opinions (higher similarity → less noisy). The averaging estimator θ_MEAN is natural for this model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family F_k(A, δ) for subjective model (assignment-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ranking now depends on assignment A, the class of 'separated' instances is assignment-dependent; theorems (Theorem 7) state recovery guarantees uniformly over this class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery guarantees for subjective-score model (Theorems 7 and 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogues of previous theorems: for monotonically decreasing h and q ∈ [λ(1−h(0)),λ], if δ exceeds a threshold depending on (λ − q τ_q), ln m, λ and α then APR4A with θ_MEAN recovers top-k (or bounds Hamming error) with high probability; converses give lower bounds. (Theorems 7,8)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PeerReview4All provides minimax guarantees both under objective-score and subjective-score models for the appropriate estimators (θ_MLE in objective, θ_MEAN in subjective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness measure Γ_S^f(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness objective Γ_S (with transformation f, typically f(s)=1−h(s) or f(s)=s): used to evaluate the worst-off paper's total transformed similarity under assignment A. (Multiple references e.g., Equation 3 context and S(q) def.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PeerReview4All explicitly optimizes fairness (minimize neglect of worst-off paper). S(q) uses fairness threshold to define similarity matrix classes. Choice of f affects algorithm behavior and approximation bounds (ILPR may perform poorly when f is unbounded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of similarities GS(A) as alternative objective
rubrics_metrics.description: GS(A) := sum of assigned similarities; TPMS aims to maximize this cumulative sum. (Section 8 introduction and experiments)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off: maximizing GS can hurt fairness (worst-off papers), which can reduce acceptance accuracy. PeerReview4All uses a max-cost heuristic to balance fairness and GS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Load constraints λ (reviewers per paper) and μ (papers per reviewer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paper must be assigned to λ reviewers; each reviewer has capacity at most μ. (Experiment setups: λ=4, μ=2 etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feasibility and approximation guarantees depend on λ and μ. Worst-case approximation factor 1/λ arises from these load constraints; algorithm implementations must enforce conflicts as additional constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worst-case approximation guarantee 1/λ for PeerReview4All
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 1 guarantees a worst-case approximation factor at least 1/λ for fairness objective; empirical τ_q often much better (e.g., ≥ 0.98 in ICLR experiment). (Multiple remarks)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should expect theoretical worst-case but often see much better practical approximation ratios; use empirical evaluation to measure τ_q on real similarity matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evaluation metrics for assignment algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics used: fairness Γ_S(A), mean sum of similarities (1/m) GS(A), fraction of papers incorrectly accepted (error fraction), ordered-sum-similarity ratios, Hamming error fraction plots across separation thresholds. (Sections 8.1–8.2 and figures/tables)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate assignments, both assignment-quality metrics (fairness, GS) and downstream selection accuracy (fraction wrongly accepted, Hamming distance) should be measured. Experiments include synthetic cases and approximated real conference similarity matrices (ICLR'18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Max-cost max-flow heuristic (implementation detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation of PeerReview4All picks max-flow with maximum cost in Step 6 of Subroutine 1 to break ties and improve average quality. (Section 8 intro and experiments)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristic helps the average quality (total sum similarity) of APR4A be close to or better than ILPR/AHARD while preserving fairness. Recommended as practical tie-breaking strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early-stopping guarantee after first iteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness guarantees of Theorem 1 are achieved after the first iteration of Steps 2 to 7 of Algorithm 1; the first-iteration assignment APR4A_1 is therefore a valid, computationally cheaper alternative. (Section 8.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In large-scale problems, one can use APR4A_1 to obtain fairness guarantees quickly; additional iterations improve fairness for the second worst-off and so on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptivity / robustness of PeerReview4All to similarity structure
rubrics_metrics.description: PeerReview4All adapts to structures of similarity matrices — from cases when optimal assignment provides only one strong reviewer for some papers to ideal cases with λ strong reviewers — ensuring even the most disadvantaged paper gets sufficient expertise. (Corollary 4 remarks and end of Section 6.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: algorithm will allocate reviewers to improve worst-off papers and maintain good average quality; corroborated by synthetic and approximate-real experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthetic scenario design for stress-testing algorithms (C1–C5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five constructed cases: (C1) Non-mainstream papers; (C2) Many weak reviewers; (C3) Few super-strong reviewers; (C4) Adverse case (hard for algorithm); (C5) Sparse similarities. (Section 8.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diverse, interpretable scenarios to reveal strengths/weaknesses: fairness vs GS trade-offs, approximation behavior, and downstream selection accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest handling
rubrics_metrics.description: In ICLR’18 approximation experiment, a conflict matrix C disallows assigning a reviewer to any paper they authored; assignments enforce these constraints. (Section 8.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments must respect conflicts; experiments demonstrate PeerReview4All can incorporate conflict constraints while optimizing fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of ILPR when f(s) unbounded
rubrics_metrics.description: ILPR algorithm's approximation guarantee (9) becomes weak when f(s)=1/(1−s) is large/unbounded, leading to poor performance in some cases (C2, C3). (Section 8.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using ILPR when the transformation f(s) is unbounded; choose f(s) compatible with algorithmic assumptions or prefer algorithms robust to unbounded f.
